The Western rattlesnake (Crotalus oreganus) exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism in its ultimate snout-vent length, with males reaching a greater maximum adult body length of 75.1 centimeters [Li = 75.1 centimeters] compared to 68.3 centimeters [Li = 68.3 centimeters] for females, a pattern commonly observed in viperids where male-male combat for mating opportunities may select for larger body size. At hatching, neonates emerge with a relatively modest snout-vent length of 27.4 centimeters [Lb = 27.4 centimeters], which represents approximately one-third to one-half of the length required to reach sexual maturity. This substantial growth trajectory from a small hatchling to a large-bodied adult necessitates a prolonged juvenile period during which individuals must forage actively and avoid predation across the diverse habitats of western North America, including grasslands, chaparral, and oak woodlands.

Detailed laboratory studies have documented the developmental milestones of Crotalus oreganus under controlled thermal regimes. When incubated at a constant temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the developmental period from oviposition to hatching lasts approximately 70 days [ab = approximately 70 days], a duration that falls within the broader range of 27 to 32 °C reported in the literature for successful embryogenesis. At the moment of hatching, neonates exhibit a wet weight at birth of 14.5 grams [Wwb = 14.5 grams], although field records indicate that this figure can range from 10 to 21 grams depending on maternal nutritional condition and local prey abundance during gestation. This relatively small birth mass belies the rapid early growth phase that follows the onset of exogenous feeding, as young snakes begin consuming small lizards and neonate rodents.

The onset of reproductive maturity in this species is strongly influenced by both sex and local environmental conditions. Under thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in Crotalus oreganus, estimated at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females reach puberty approximately 3 years after birth [tp = approximately 3 years after birth], a protracted interval that reflects the substantial energy reserves required to support vitellogenesis and gestation. Males, in contrast, mature more rapidly, achieving sexual maturity approximately 2 years after birth [tp = approximately 2 years after birth] under the same at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]thermal regime. This earlier maturation in males is consistent with a mating system where smaller, younger males can successfully locate and court receptive females, whereas females must attain a larger body size to accommodate clutch production.

The snout-vent length at puberty further underscores these sex-specific life history strategies, with females typically reaching reproductive maturity at 58.8 centimeters [Lp = 58.8 centimeters] while males become capable of breeding at a smaller body length of 51.8 centimeters [Lp = 51.8 centimeters]. This difference in size at maturity aligns with the ultimate body size dimorphism observed between the sexes. Reproductive output is relatively low compared to many colubrids; females produce 3 to 8 young per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 8 young per clutch], and based on field mark-recapture studies conducted at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], most individuals produce 1 clutch every 2 years [F_R_i = 1 clutch every 2 years], resulting in a modest maximum reproductive rate. Such infrequent reproduction likely reflects the high energetic costs of viviparity in a temperate-zone pitviper.

In terms of overall longevity, captive records for Western rattlesnake indicate that individuals maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] can attain a maximum lifespan of approximately 24 years [am = approximately 24 years], placing this species among the longer-lived viperids. The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult females in the field averages 226.9 grams [Wwi = 226.9 grams], whereas adult males reach a substantially greater asymptotic body mass of 279.3 grams [Wwi = 279.3 grams], a difference that exceeds what would be predicted from skeletal size alone. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in mass, coupled with the delayed female maturation, suggests that female reproductive success is more strongly constrained by body size and energy storage capacity than in males, with larger females capable of producing larger litters in the occasional years when they do reproduce.
